Dimensionless scalars abound. But if I use a mach number in place of blood alcohol, or a coefficient of friction in place of Pi I get nonsense. It seems these numbers have a dimension, but they don't.

On my can of beer it says 5.8% alcohol by volume. The 5.8% is dimensionless, yet "by volume" is still an important property of that 5.8%. Without the "by volume", 5.8% would mean nothing. It's like a dimension, but it can't be. Math doesn't lie and those dimensions canceled.

What is this "by volume" phenomena called? Does it have a name?
What is the "by volume" in alcohol content? In general, any dimensionless quantity.

The percent itself has no dimension. The ‘by volume’ is simply telling you how the percentage was calculated. It could be a mass percentage, molar percentage, or any number of others. So a percent without context is useless, that doesn’t give it a dimension.

Unfortunately most of these kind of values have a historical context. Humans just refuse to adapt sometimes.

Maybe the word is "constraint" or "relationship" if you want to play semantic games. The whole thing constitutes a "measurement"

I can play this game too: "5 meters is a meaningless dimension because you must first define what is a meter, if I put in 5 megapascals I don't know how wide this room is"
It's not meaningless because a meter is defined and more importantly, doesn't cancel out. In the case I'm talking about the dimensions cancel formally so it wouldn't matter if they were defined.

But it doesn't cancel, does it? Think about what the real parts of it are. It's volume alcohol divided by volume liquid, which is

(volume alcohol)/(volume alcohol + volume other stuff)

If you have 5% abv pure alcohol dissolved in pure water, and you have 20g of this liquid, how much alcohol do you have? Hint the answer's not 1ml or 1g. If you didn't have ABV specified then it really is dimensionless and the answer could be 1g if it was alcohol by mass.
could it be different densities maybe? Maybe it is indicating % by volume, not weight?
Could be, but then the % by weight is different than % by volume. So even though the volume cancelled, we had to remember "by volume" anyway.

Show your work and I can more easily point out why the volume mattered, if my example problem didn't help. The idea is with multivariable algebra you are doing substitutions, and you would solve

0.05 = Va/Vt

Vt = Va + Vo

and whatever else you needed to get to your answer. You can see I already skipped a step earlier, going straight to

0.05 = Va/(Va +Vt)

When you do problems, try this. Box off part of the space above your working area and make 3 columns. Put in direct numbers you know in one, in the example I gave, you'd put 20g = Mt. Put in formulas provided in another, like 0.05 = Va/Vt. Put in book equations and constants in the other, in my example you'd use density of alcohol and density of water. Below that write down the variable you are solving for. I didn't specify mass or volume for your answer, and the reason is you need to be able to express one in terms of the other in order to answer the question anyway.

With all that, you're ready to ask yourself "how do I write an equation to express this variable in terms of these other things?"
